newsitem.title: USA: Defense Secretary Perry to leave Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: Defense Secretary Perry to leave Pentagon.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry has told President Bill Clinton he plans to resign and could leave the Cabinet within a few months when a successor is chosen, defence officials said on Wednesday.
One of the officials, who asked not to be identified, said Perry told his staff early on Wednesday he had told Clinton he wanted to return to private life after nearly three years on the job.

The news that Perry, 69, planned to leave after Clinton's re-election on Tuesday came on the heels of statements from State Department officials that Secretary of State Warren Christopher planned to resign his post within days.

Perry is considered by many experts to be one of the strongest and most popular Pentagon leaders in decades despite recent controversy over the future role of U.S. forces in Bosnia, the possible effects of Iraqi chemical weapons on U.S. Gulf War troops and responsibility for two bomb attacks in Saudi Arabia that killed 24 American troops.

He told his staff on Tuesday before departing on a two-day trip to Nebraska and Colorado that he had no definite date to leave but expected to stay on for at least a few months until a successor was appointed by Clinton.

Published reports about a possible successor to Perry have centred on CIA Director John Deutch, who served as deputy defence secretary under Perry until he moved to the Central Intelligence Agency last year.

"I don't think there is any good time or bad time walking away from the job as secretary of defence," Perry told reporters who travelled with him to Europe last month. "There is always a problem. There is always a crisis. There's always some programme that is halfway completed."

Perry, who has nurtured close ties with senior defence officials in Russia and other former Soviet communist states, rose from the post of deputy defence secretary in early 1994 to take the top job after the late Defence Secretary Les Aspin resigned under pressure.
Since then he has undertaken a crushing work and travel schedule that would leave many less active persons exhausted.

There was no immediate indication of who might succeed Perry, but published reports have speculated around Deutch and retiring Georgia Sen. Sam Nunn, former chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Retiring Republican Sen. William Cohen of Maine has also emerged in reports as a possible candidate. Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, who previosuly served as the Pentagon's top lawyer, has made no secret that she would like the job.

Perry, in response to questions from reporters in the interview last month, expressed pride in initiatives under him to slash Cold War nuclear weapons in the United States and former Soviet Union, to improve support for military personnel and dependents and reform the way the Pentagon buys arms and equipment to save billions of dollars.

"Whenever I leave the defence department, I would like to be able to look back and say first of all (that) I have done something significant and, secondly, many of the long-term programmes that I have worked on will continue long after I leave," he said.

"I should, for point of reference, say that I had not decided to take this job in the first place. It was not something I sought, something I was anxious to do," said Perry. "It was something which was urged on me and after a lot of consideration I finally decided to do."
